description: Complete game audio knowledge - spatial audio, middleware integration, procedural audio, adaptive music, and sound design

sections.name: Spatial Audio & 3D Sound
sections.explanation_simple: Spatial audio makes sounds feel like they come from a specific direction. When an enemy is to your left, you hear the gunshot in your left ear, and it gets louder as you turn toward them. This works through HRTF (Head Related Transfer Function) - the shape of your ears and head changes how sound reaches your eardrums depending on direction. Game audio engines simulate this. It's the difference between 'hearing a sound' and 'feeling where that sound came from' - critical for immersion and competitive gaming.
key_concepts: HRTF: How ear shape changes sound based on direction
Attenuation: Sound gets quieter over distance
Doppler Effect: Sound pitch changes as source moves past you (race cars, bullets)
Occlusion: Sound muffled when behind walls
Reverb Zones: Different echo in different rooms (cave vs hall)
Audio Raycasting: Tracing sound paths like light for realistic acoustics
Ambisonics: Full-sphere surround sound for VR

sections.name: Adaptive Music Systems
sections.explanation_simple: Adaptive music changes based on what's happening in the game. When you're fighting a boss, the music gets intense. When you enter a calm village, it becomes peaceful. When enemies are chasing you, drums kick in. This is done in two ways: 1) Horizontal resequencing - swapping between different music tracks (exploration, combat, boss), and 2) Vertical layering - adding/subtracting instrument layers (just strings, then add drums, then add brass). Games like Zelda: Breath of the Wild and DOOM use adaptive music brilliantly.
key_concepts: Horizontal Resequencing: Switching between different composed segments
Vertical Layering: Adding/removing instrument tracks on the fly
Stingers: Short musical hits for events (level up, enemy death, discovery)
Transition: Music that plays when switching between states
Beat Matching: Keeping musical timing when switching layers
MIDI vs Audio: MIDI is synthesized (more flexible), audio is pre-recorded (higher quality)
FMOD Event System: Game triggers events, audio middleware handles transitions

sections.name: Sound Design for Games
sections.explanation_simple: Sound design is creating all the audio in a game - not just music, but every footstep, gunshot, UI click, and ambient bird chirp. Good sound design is invisible (you don't notice it), but bad sound design makes the game feel 'off'. Every action in a game needs a matching sound. The trick is layering - a single gunshot might be 3-5 sounds mixed together: the initial crack, the mechanical slide, the shell casing hitting the ground, and the reverb from the room. Sound designers record real sounds (foley) or synthesize them.
key_concepts: Foley: Recording real-world sounds for game use
Layering: Combining multiple sounds to create one rich sound
Sound Synthesis: Creating sounds with oscillators, filters, envelopes
Granular Synthesis: Slicing sound into tiny grains, rearranging them
Compression: Making sounds sit well together in the mix
EQ: Shaping frequencies (bass, mids, treble)
Reverb: Adding space/room feel to sounds
Dynamic Range: Difference between quietest and loudest sounds
